in_text_mentions: plaques with fine follicular scaling over bilateral cheeks and lateral aspect of bilateral upper eyelids, sparing the nasolabial folds and nose (Figure 1a, b). Dermoscopic examination revealed white conical-shaped filaments protruding from follicular openings suggestive of Demodex ‘tails’, a finding specific for demodicosis, and nonspecific superficial scales (Figure 2). A clinical diagnosis of pigmented demodicosis was made. Differential diagnoses included seborrhoeic dermatitis, contact dermatitis and pemphigus foliaceus/erythematosus. Fungal scrape for microscopy and culture were negative.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Low-power H&E skin biopsy from a 65-year-old man with demodicosis; shows orthokeratotic epidermis, follicular hyperkeratosis and perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, supporting folliculitis due to Demodex. B: Higher-power H&E of follicular units with perifollicular lymphocytic inflammation and intrafollicular Demodex mites, consistent with demodicosis. C: High-power H&E showing Demodex mites within a follicular unit, the diagnostic histologic hallmark of demodicosis.
panels.attribution_text: Moran et al. Diagnostic Challenges of Demodicosis in a 65-Year-Old Man: A Case of Chronic Pruritus.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.86764. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Dermatological histopathological report corresponding to a skin biopsy. The biopsy reveals a skin sample showing orthokeratotic epidermis with basket-weave stratum corneum and dermis containing superficial and perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates. There is perifollicular inflammation rich in lymphocytes without atypia, along with histiocytes. Within the follicular unit, structures consistent with Demodex mites are observed, identifiable by their characteristic elongated bodies and segmented exoskeletons. A special stain (PAS) was performed to rule out other microorganisms, yielding a negative result. The diagnosis is folliculitis due to Demodex.

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of a human patient's nipple/areola with black arrows marking the scaling (and erythema) described in the caption and in-text ('erythema and scaling were noted around the areola of both nipples'). The article is specifically titled 'Asymptomatic Bilateral Demodicosis of the Nipple' and the figure is captioned as the clinical manifestation of that condition, so attribution to demodicosis is directly supported. Scaling maps to the vocabulary finding 'pityriasiform scaling'; the erythema is areolar rather than facial, so it is listed as a proposed finding. Nipple involvement is an uncommon site for demodicosis (variant).

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of the occipital scalp of a patient in whom skin biopsy showed excessive Demodex mites in the follicular infundibulum, establishing the diagnosis of scalp demodicosis; the article title explicitly describes this as an atypical localization of demodicosis. The panel shows the captioned diffuse erythema with erythematous papules and hair thinning, a real patient image without third-party copyright concerns. [raw subtype: scalp demodicosis (atypical localization)]

panels.figure_caption: Diffuse erythema with erythematous papules associated with hair thinning in the occipital scalp
in_text_mentions: appearing 10 days after a moderate SARS‐CoV‐2 infection. The skin examination found many firm and erythematous papules on a background of a diffuse erythema associated with hair thinning in the occipital region (Figure 1). Skin biopsy revealed excessive Demodex mites in the follicular infundibulum (Figure 2B) with perivascular and perifollicular lymphocytic infiltration (Figure 2A). Based on the clinical and histopathological data, the diagnosis of scalp demodicosis was retained. The patient was treated with topical metronidazole. A complete regression of the lesions was obtained in two weeks.
